m4-t1.question: Why did the lower-bidding bakery win more ad placements at a lower cost per click?
options: The platform favoured small businesses
The auction ranks Bid × Quality — its relevant ad and matching landing page outranked the higher bid and paid just enough to beat the runner-up
It advertised during off-peak hours
The higher bidder ran out of budget
m4-t1.explanation: Ad Rank = Bid × Quality; relevance wins at a discount because most auctions charge just enough to beat the ad below you.

m4-t1.question: Which is a legitimate job for paid media?
options: Fixing a weak offer by exposing it to more people
Capturing existing intent, creating awareness fast, retargeting the almost-convinced, and testing messages cheaply
Replacing the need for a website
Guaranteeing first-page organic rankings
m4-t1.explanation: Paid is rented, precisely targeted attention — a multiplier that exposes weak offers faster, not a foundation.

m4-t1.question: A campaign with a CPM buying model is most appropriate when the goal is…
options: Enquiries from search
Cart-abandoner recovery
Awareness and reach — launches and brand-building
Cost per action optimisation
m4-t1.explanation: CPC buys visits, CPM buys awareness, CPA needs trusted conversion tracking — match the model to the funnel stage.

m4-t1.question: ₹6,000 budget, estimated CPC ₹12, expected landing conversion 4%. What is the cost per acquisition?
m4-t1.explanation: 500 clicks × 4% = 20 conversions; ₹6,000 ÷ 20 = ₹300 CPA. Run this chain before launch, not after the invoice.

m4-t1.question: What does the lesson call the classic sign of bidding more to fix a bad ad?
options: A quality score bonus
Paying a stupidity premium — quality is the cheaper lever
An auction penalty
Improved organic rankings
m4-t1.explanation: Outbidding a rival to compensate for a mismatched ad is paying extra for the privilege of being ignored.

m4-t2.question: What is the test of a well-formed ad group?
options: It contains at least 100 keywords
Every keyword in it could share one ad and one landing page
It targets all of India
It uses only broad match keywords
m4-t2.explanation: Tight themes let one ad match every keyword — raising relevance, which lowers cost. If not, split the ad group.

m4-t2.question: Which match type gives the widest reach with the greatest waste risk?
options: Exact match
Phrase match
Broad match
Negative match
m4-t2.explanation: Broad match triggers on related searches — volume without control, survivable only with a maintained negative-keyword list.

m4-t2.question: Where does the lesson say wasted budgets are reclaimed?
options: In raising quality scores
In negative keywords and the weekly search-terms review
In switching platforms
In lowering all bids
m4-t2.explanation: Reading what you actually paid for and pruning it is the fastest marketing education and the biggest quick win.

m4-t2.question: A search ad's Headline 1 should…
options: Show the brand name and founding year
Mirror the query, with a specific number or differentiator in the other headlines
Contain a clever pun to stand out
List as many products as fit in 30 characters
m4-t2.explanation: Search ads reward mirror-the-query clarity: the searcher must see their own words reflected, then the specifics that answer the next question.

m4-t2.question: High CTR but poor conversion rate. Where is the problem, and what is the fix?
options: The ad — rewrite the headlines
The bid — lower it to buy better traffic
The landing page — the click's promise is not being kept on the page
The platform — switch to another network
m4-t2.explanation: CTR is the market's verdict on the ad; conversion rate is the page's verdict. Diagnose before adjusting.

m4-t3.question: What is the fundamental difference between search ads and social/display/video ads?
options: Social ads are always cheaper
Search captures existing intent; the others must interrupt attention that asked for nothing
Social ads cannot target by location
Search ads cannot contain images
m4-t3.explanation: Interruption media earns attention relevant to the moment, not to a query — a different psychology and craft.

m4-t3.question: For a small budget, what is the professional audience sequence?
options: Core audiences first, then retargeting, then lookalikes
Retargeting first, lookalikes second, sharp core audiences last
Lookalikes only, until they convert
All three equally from day one
m4-t3.explanation: Retargeting gives the cheapest conversions, lookalikes scale with the algorithm's best knowledge, core is the starting point only when sharp.

m4-t3.question: In a retargeting sequence, why must the converted be excluded?
options: To reduce the audience size for faster delivery
So buyers stop seeing requests to buy — budget moves to the unconvinced, and the brand stops looking oblivious
Because platforms forbid advertising to customers
To reset the frequency counter
m4-t3.explanation: Sequencing works when each message meets a person at their stage; the converted belong in a different journey (Module 7).

m4-t3.question: The 3-second rule for video ads means…
options: The ad must be three seconds long
The video must prove its relevance in the first three seconds — product visible, promise legible, sound optional
Bidding happens every three seconds
Viewers decide costs after three seconds
m4-t3.explanation: If the logo appears before the story, you have paid to be skipped; most feeds are muted, so design for silence.

m4-t3.question: Why does the lesson say 'the creative is the targeting' on modern social platforms?
options: Creative replaces the need for budgets
Algorithms decide who sees the ad largely from who engages with it — a blurry message finds a blurry audience
Targeting options were removed from platforms
Creative controls the auction bid automatically
m4-t3.explanation: Delivery systems learn from engagement signals; a precise, native, single-idea creative attracts precisely the audience it deserves.

m4-t4.question: 1,100 clicks produced 9 enquiries on an eleven-field form. What does the lesson identify as the real economics problem?
options: The ad targeting was too broad
The landing page — message mismatch, hidden fees, and form friction taxed the conversion
The CPC was too high
The campaign needed a bigger budget
m4-t4.explanation: The destination decides the campaign's economics: one promise, the answer above the fold, three fields, no exits.

m4-t4.question: What is 'message match' on a landing page?
options: Using the same font as the ad
The headline completing the sentence the ad started — same words, same promise
Matching the competitor's messaging
Translating the ad into Kannada
m4-t4.explanation: 'B.Com with CA coaching' in the ad must appear as the page's H1; mismatched pages leak money silently.

m4-t4.question: What is the non-negotiable launch order?
options: Ads → tracking → page
Tracking → ads → page
Page → tracking → ads
Ads → page → tracking
m4-t4.explanation: You cannot retro-fit data you never collected: define the conversion, install and TEST the tag, UTM every link, then launch.

m4-t4.question: Week one: CPA per ad group computed. What is the standard ritual?
options: Raise all bids to improve delivery
Pause the worst ~20%, move budget to the best, check frequency, and audit the page against the assumed conversion rate
Restart the campaign from scratch
Wait three more weeks before changing anything
m4-t4.explanation: Prune waste, reinforce winners, and when conversion underperforms the assumption, the page is the project — not the ads.

m4-t4.question: What does a UTM like utm_campaign=admissions-oct&utm_content=adgroup-dumbbells buy you?
options: Lower CPCs on those ads
Attribution in analytics that survives to the exact ad group, independent of platform reporting
Automatic negative keywords
Priority in the ad auction
m4-t4.explanation: UTMs make traffic self-describing — Module 6's dashboards and honest attribution depend on them.

questions.question: Client: ₹15,000 budget, CPC estimate ₹10, page converts at 2%, average order value ₹900 with no repeat purchase. What is the honest recommendation?
options: Launch — 1,500 clicks is strong visibility
Do not launch yet: the arithmetic yields 30 orders and ₹500 CPA against ₹900 value — margins are too thin; fix the page or the offer first
Launch with broad match to increase volume
Spend the budget on one day for momentum
questions.explanation: 1,500 × 2% = 30 orders; ₹15,000 ÷ 30 = ₹500 CPA against ₹900 one-time value leaves nothing for product or operations — fix the economics before buying traffic.

questions.question: A campaign shows: CTR 6%, CPC ₹9, conversion rate 0.4%. Which diagnosis and action are correct?
options: The ads are failing — rewrite headlines
The ads are winning clicks; the page is losing them — rebuild the landing experience (message match, friction, speed) before touching the ads
Raise bids to reach better users
Switch from CPC to CPM buying
questions.explanation: Strong CTR with weak conversion is the classic page problem: the click's promise is not being kept at the destination.

questions.question: A gym-equipment seller wants 'gym' as a broad-match keyword with no negatives. What will the search-terms report most likely show, and what is the fix?
options: Relevant traffic only; no fix needed
Wasted spend on 'gym tips', 'free workout plans', 'gym jobs' — add negatives (free, tips, jobs, how to, used) and structure product-line ad groups
Higher Quality Score from broad reach
Lower CPC because of volume
questions.explanation: Broad match without a negative shield is a budget vacuum; negatives plus tight ad-group themes reclaim it.

questions.question: A ₹10,000 social plan allocates 70% to a broad core audience and 30% to retargeting. The site gets 400 visits/month. What is the professional critique?
options: The split is correct — retargeting audiences are always too small
It is inverted for this stage: retargeting the 400 warm visitors converts cheapest; scale cold only after the message is proven on them
Retargeting requires a minimum of 50,000 visitors
Both audiences should be merged into one campaign
questions.explanation: Retargeting first (cheapest conversions, proof of message), lookalikes/core second once the creative has earned its evidence.

questions.question: The enquiry form asks 11 fields including 'mother's occupation'. Post-launch, what single change is most likely to move CPA the most?
options: Increasing the daily budget by 50%
Cutting the form to three fields (name, phone, programme) and moving everything else to the follow-up call
Adding more ad extensions
Changing the bid strategy to maximise clicks
questions.explanation: Every field is a tax on conversion; the rebuilt page in the lesson moved 9 enquiries to 240 with exactly this change plus message match.

questions.question: A team launches ads on Monday and 'optimises' aggressively on Tuesday. What principle are they violating?
options: The frequency cap rule
Auction algorithms need a learning period; judge pacing on day 2–3 and performance at week one, with the page as first suspect
The 3-second rule
The negative keyword rule
questions.explanation: Day-one judgements react to noise; the launch-week ritual exists to let signal accumulate before decisions.

questions.question: Which UTM set is best practice for a search campaign with two ad groups?
options: utm_source=google on all links; nothing else
source=google, medium=cpc, campaign=admissions-oct, content=adgroup-dumbbells vs adgroup-benches — consistent naming that survives to the ad group
The same UTM on every ad including social campaigns
No UTMs — the platform reports everything
questions.explanation: UTMs make traffic self-describing and cross-checkable in analytics, independent of any single platform's reporting.

questions.question: A video ad shows the logo for 4 seconds before the product appears. Sound is on-screen-free. What are the two faults?
options: Too long and too cheap
Logo-before-story breaks the 3-second rule, and relying on audio ignores muted feeds — the promise must be legible in silence
Wrong aspect ratio and platform
No CTA and no UTM
questions.explanation: The first three seconds must prove relevance: product visible, promise legible, sound optional.

questions.question: Retargeting frequency has climbed to 8 with flat results. What does the lesson advise?
options: Raise the bid to refresh delivery
Rotate fresh creative and/or cap frequency — past the sweet spot (~5), repetition breeds irritation and rising costs
Broaden the retargeting window to 180 days
Exclude the audience and stop retargeting forever
questions.explanation: Frequency has a sweet spot; when it climbs with flat results, refresh the message rather than repeat it louder.

questions.question: Which launch-day item is most often skipped and most expensive to skip?
options: Setting the campaign name
Testing that the conversion tag actually fires on a submission before spending
Choosing the campaign's time zone
Writing three headlines instead of two
questions.explanation: An untested tag is a story, not tracking — a week of optimisation blind, discovered only after the invoice.
